Teacher Abuse

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
For parents, school is the safest environment for their children, but for some children within the South African school system this comes at a price... the value is the depth of their scars

Unique Selling Point:
For parents, school is the safest possible environment for their children. Some teachers across the country have violated that trust, as the caregiver has become the abuser in some of our schools in South Africa.

Summary:
The Centre for Justice and Crime Prevention’s 2012 School Violence study found that up to 73% of children were still being beaten by their teachers and in 2017, this is still an ongoing crisis in our schools.

Recently cellphone footage has surfaced with teachers abusing students in classrooms. For over 20 years corporal punishment has been outlawed as a form of enforcing discipline at schools. But some teachers across South Africa have continued to break the law.


Further information:
Video clips of teachers caning and smacking students in class even going as far as using abusive language to some students have gone viral. In one of the most extreme cases, a video clip shows teachers in the KZN including the school principal sexually assaulting a female student. The department of education has condemned all these acts of violence by the teachers, but is that enough?

Tshepiso Monnakgotla mentions that since her child was publicly beaten and humiliated by her school’s food handler, she has had no communication with the department and her child has been suffering ever since with trauma and not being able sleep. Her child needs counseling and the department hasn’t come fourth with any help 3 weeks later.

Although a few video clips surfaced, there might be more of these incidents that do not get recorded or reported. But the abuse and videos going viral can cause an even bigger psychological trauma to the children. For many of these children it is trauma that will haunt them for many years to come.

How will the department deal with the ongoing issue abuse in schools? Are these acts of violence a product of our state of being as a society and who is accountable when these incidents occur? Carte Blanche investigates

Tshepiso Monnakgotla is the mother of a 16-year-old mentally ill girl who was attacked by her school’s food handler in Soweto. Tshepiso says both her and her daughter have been traumatised by the incident to an extent where her daughter doesn’t sleep or eat and she is scared of going back to school. No one can tell her why her daughter was beaten up and the department hasn’t offered her any kind of help with counseling for her daughter.

Kristy and Shane Kreusch reported a teacher that has been victimizing and beating up their child to the education department in the Eastern cape but nothing has been done. They even opened a case with the police but they could not be helped. The department told them that the teacher, Ms Hill is a good teacher and perhaps her behavior is linked to her loneliness. The department in the province does however admit to having numerous complains about the teacher but they cannot explain why they haven’t done anything about her.


We We speak to the national department of basic education’s spokesperson Mr Elijah Mhlanga who has condemned this acts of abuse on students and says the department will take appropriate actions with these teachers. He speaks of how often such incidents get reported to them and how they normally deal with them. What does this do to the image of the schooling system and most importantly how do they deal with the victims once post the abuse?

Carol Bower is an experienced child activist based in Cape Town; she believes condemning these actions is just not enough. More needs to be done to ensure the safety of the children. According to Carol many believe that there is no other way to discipline a child other than a beating and that is not ok. Being hit in childhood has been linked to negative physical, psycho-social, emotional, behavioral and cognitive outcomes. The most disturbing part is this can be linked to the society we live in, with the country having one of the highest levels of violence in the world, it seems our only response to anything we do not like is to lash out.

We also speak to parents of a pupil that was beaten up by a teacher and her hand is now permanently damaged. Siphokazi tyalidikazi is currently 15 years of age. When she was 13 her teacher beat her up for not finishing her homework and now her right hand is permanently disabled. She can no longer write with her right hand as a result and had to adjust to write with her left. The teacher that abused her was fined and allowed to nget back to work. She had to change schools because once her parents pressed charges she got victimized at the school by teachers at emfuleni primary school. The parents are now suing the department of education and holding them accountable for the incident. This is currently an ongoing case.

Themba Ndlovu of the South African council of educators believes that this is a huge dent to the profession and creates a bad image for profession. The council is responsible for investigations into these incidents and according to Themba they have received 21 complaints of sexual assault from April this up to now, this according to Themba is one too many and needs to stop. The council is engaging with stakeholders and teachers unions to discourage corporal punishment and any kind of abuse, as they believe it will take a collective to eradicate this behavior.

Press Release:


Teacher Abuse
Corporal punishment has been outlawed for over 20 years in South African schools, but it seems
it is still the most prominent form of discipline. In recent weeks, horrific images of teachers
violently caning and abusing pupils have gone viral. The Department of Basic Education has
condemned this, but have they done enough to remedy the situation? Carte Blanche asks: what
happens when the educator becomes the abuser?

Script:


Montage of video's of children being beaten

Link: Horrific images of teachers violently attacking students have gone viral in recent weeks. This has put a spot light on our schools and the safety of our children is in question

Sphokazi: My hand was painful and i was afraid to tell the teacher that it is painful.

Nthabiseng: She came to me and started hitting me with her shoes, after that they tried to stop her but she pinned me down onto the seat and started beating me.

Link: These are the buses that transport children with special needs, it was in one of these buses when Nthabiseng was beaten and assaulted by the food handler.

VO: The driver then takes over from the food handler who is supervising and physically throws this helpless child out of the bus, he is assisted by another school pupil.

Carol: There is a crime been committed.

VO: Carol Bower has been involved in Child protection for over 30 years.

Carol: the children act says that people who are unfit to work with children are not allowed to work with them.

VO: These children have been physically and emotionally scarred by their teachers, in a festering culture of violence within South African schools. Deputy director General of Education Dr Granville Whittle condemns these acts

Whittle: It's often that culturally within communities corporal punishment is accepted as a means of discipline in children

Carol: Corporal punishment is one of several forms of violence that is happening in our schools. Theres bullying, sexual abuse, a number of other kinds of violence being perpetrated by learners but also against them and violence feeds violence.

VO: Recent reports of a security guard who sexually molested 87 learners has shocked the country and currently the South African Council of Educators has over 100 complaints of corporal punishment and 21 cases of sexual abuse since April, says Themba Ndlovu.

McFarlane: Thats nowhere near what is actually happening at schools

Themba: Nowhere near what is happening because of under reporting.

VO: Even when Tshepiso, Nthabiseng's mother reported the bus incident, she had no assistance from the school.

Tshepiso: The school hasn't called me. No one from school came to me, called me, asked me about my daughter how is she doing, asked me about the case.

VO: After being beaten and thrown off the bus in Meadowlands Soweto, Nthabiseng who is a special needs child, had to walk home through the busy streets for about one and a half kilometers.

Nthabiseng: As I was crossing the street, on the second jump I ended up getting dizzy. I ended feeling like i was seeing that woman again beating me while I was screaming.

Macfarlane: Please tell me what happened on the bus.

Nthabiseng: I was defending myself because the matron lady and the driver have never liked me at the school. They think I'm mentally disabled and crazy. I end up wanting to kill myself, I don't understand what is going on and what I did to them.

VO: Nthabiseng had meningitis as a baby and has a permanent tube draining fluid from her head, since then her epileptic fits have increased.

Tshepiso: She is not the same child anymore Every night I'm sleeping with her just the two of us. She is not sleeping. she will open her eyes like this for the whole night.

Link: For over 20 years corporal punishment has been outlawed in south african schools yet it is still the most prominent form of discipline and for some students the scars last a lifetime

VO: In the Western Cape at Nal'Nkamva Primary School in Mfuleni, then 13 year old Spokhazi's right hand was crippled by her teacher Ms Fadane, when she beat her with a pipe.

Sphokazi: It makes me feel bad because I wasn't born like this without an arm because i might as well be disabled now. I can't do anything. I'm now different from other kids.

Macfarlane: So you can't even hold things with your hand?

Sphokazi: Yes

Sphokazi: Yes. I can only raise it up to here and the it gets sore in this area(pointing at neck

VO: Nobantu Tyhalidikazi, Sphokazi's mother, is devastated.

Nobantu: She cannot do anything for herself, because it's her right hand that she writes with. it's also important that I fix her up in the morning, bathe her.

VO: After her parents complained to the school the teacher was suspended for two weeks and then reinstated with an R8000 fine.

Carol: If i assault you i can go to jail. A 2 week suspension and a fine is not consequence.
The teacher should not be teaching, certainly not at the same school. She has damaged somebody
imagine going back into the class of the person who did that to you?

Themba: Our learners must not learn out of fear, because corporal punishment is instilling fear in learning. Children need to be motivated to learn.

VO: Sphokazi had to change schools because she was being victimised. Her parents are currently suing the Department of Education as they have received very little assistance

Nobantu: I was in a crisis with medical bills. They say that the funds are depleted so we can't help Siphokazi.

Themba: I cannot answer for the department, however as a citizen i believe the department should take responsibility. SACE would take up this matter with the Western Cape Department of Education. to say we have a learner sitting out there, we have parents sitting with medical bills.

VO: If a child is hit with a pipe and maimed for life, the The Department is clear on the punishment that should be meted to a teacher.

Whittle: Dismissal. It's simple. Dismissal and criminal charges. That's what we want.

VO: But this was not the case for Siphokazi's teacher.

Nobantu: The Principal said that he understand what has happened but because he is an acting principal there wasn't much he can do.

VO: The principal of a school is the link between the learners and the Department of Education and is responsible for the ultimate well being and safety of the children, but many principals are not willing to to take teachers to task.
Even in Nthabiseng's case, the principal tried to distance himself from the bus beating.

Tshepiso: He said to me you can go, this is not for the school. You can go open a case for her. then i said what do you mean and he said I don't want to be involved.

VO: This story was featured in other media and the department said they would take action, but nothing has materialised. It was only after Carte Blanche got involved that the principal called Tshepiso to a meeting, saying he wanted to apologise.

We followed Tshepiso to the meeting but the principal said he was not mandated to speak to us. We wanted to ask him some critical questions like, - why was the bus driver still at the school? Why was the food handler only dismissed and why he could not give Thsepiso their names when she wanted to lay criminal charges against them?

Principal: – This is damaging us, we are trying by all means to build our image, we can't be seen to be talking to the media, more especially with the issue that's been taken over by the department of education.

McFarlane: They've seen the video and gone on television to speak about the issue, but nothing gets done.

Themba: We are saying to the department you have made pronouncements that you are going to attend to this matter, can that leadership account for what happened because whatever happens in the school environment the principal remains accountable.

Whittle: Every single case of sexual abuse or corporal punishment must be reportedWe will no hesitate to act against principals in particular that are aware of corporal punishment happening at their school or sexual abuse

Themba: we are not seeing these reports coming through from all provinces as they should
VO: Carte Blanche was following another case in the Eastern Cape, at De Vos Malan High School where Seth, a grade 8 learner was beaten by a teacher Ms Hill.

Seth: Sound up what happened.
VO: To date Ms Hill has had several complaints leveled against her for hitting learners, but no disciplinary measures have been taken against her according to Seth's father Shane Kreusch.

Father: The time delay from when the incident happened till now, nothing has happened.
VO: On the day Carte Blanche arrived to interview the family, an urgent meeting was called by the school principal and the HOD of the province of the Eastern Cape, Mr Piens who is also the ex Principal of De Vos Malan High School.

Doorstop of Mr Piens at the car:
I cant speak to you I work for the department.

Father: the department of Eduction is more concerned about Ms Hill apologising for her actions. We want action taken and they saying process has begun, we want to know what process and miss Hill is still in the class.

Themba: If theres assault theres the criminal aspect. You may face a charge by the department who is your employer. A teacher may face a charge with us as council. A teacher may face a charge criminally because you would've broken the law.

Carol: The long term consequences cost wise for a country include that the Spokazi's of the world may never hold down a proper job.
Macfarlane: Would you like her to apologise? What would you like to see happen to the teacher?

Sphokazi: Cries

Carol: then we have a negative impact on our society and we see now the consequences of that kind of violence.

Her parents are currently suing the Department of Education as they have received very little assistance Nobantu: I was in a crisis with medical bills. They say that the funds are depleted so we can't help Siphokazi. Themba: I cannot answer for the department, however as a citizen i believe the department should take responsibility. SACE would take up this matter with the Western Cape Department of Education. to say we have a learner sitting out there, we have parents sitting with medical bills. VO: If a child is hit with a pipe and maimed for life, the The Department is clear on the punishment that should be meted to a teacher. Whittle: Dismissal. It's simple. Dismissal and criminal charges. That's what we want. VO: But this was not the case for Siphokazi's teacher. Nobantu: The Principal said that he understand what has happened but because he is an acting principal there wasn't much he can do. VO: The principal of a school is the link between the learners and the Department of Education and is responsible for the ultimate well being and safety of the children, but many principals are not willing to to take teachers to task. Even in Nthabiseng's case, the principal tried to distance himself from the bus beating. Tshepiso: He said to me you can go, this is not for the school. You can go open a case for her. then i said what do you mean and he said I don't want to be involved. VO: This story was featured in other media and the department said they would take action, but nothing has materialised. It was only after Carte Blanche got involved that the principal called Tshepiso to a meeting, saying he wanted to apologise. We followed Tshepiso to the meeting but the principal said he was not mandated to speak to us. We wanted to ask him some critical questions like, - why was the bus driver still at the school? Why was the food handler only dismissed and why he could not give Thsepiso their names when she wanted to lay criminal charges against them? Principal: – This is damaging us, we are trying by all means to build our image, we can't be seen to be talking to the media, more especially with the issue that's been taken over by the department of education. McFarlane: They've seen the video and gone on television to speak about the issue, but nothing gets done. Themba: We are saying to the department you have made pronouncements that you are going to attend to this matter, can that leadership account for what happened because whatever happens in the school environment the principal remains accountable. Whittle: Every single case of sexual abuse or corporal punishment must be reportedWe will no hesitate to act against principals in particular that are aware of corporal punishment happening at their school or sexual abuse Themba: we are not seeing these reports coming through from all provinces as they should VO: Carte Blanche was following another case in the Eastern Cape, at De Vos Malan High School where Seth, a grade 8 learner was beaten by a teacher Ms Hill. Seth: Sound up what happened. VO: To date Ms Hill has had several complaints leveled against her for hitting learners, but no disciplinary measures have been taken against her according to Seth's father Shane Kreusch. Father: The time delay from when the incident happened till now, nothing has happened. VO: On the day Carte Blanche arrived to interview the family, an urgent meeting was called by the school principal and the HOD of the province of the Eastern Cape, Mr Piens who is also the ex Principal of De Vos Malan High School. Doorstop of Mr Piens at the car: I cant speak to you I work for the department. Father: the department of Eduction is more concerned about Ms Hill apologising for her actions. We want action taken and they saying process has begun, we want to know what process and miss Hill is still in the class. Themba: If theres assault theres the criminal aspect. You may face a charge by the department who is your employer. A teacher may face a charge with us as council. A teacher may face a charge criminally because you would've broken the law. Carol: The long term consequences cost wise for a country include that the Spokazi's of the world may never hold down a proper job. Macfarlane: Would you like her to apologise? What would you like to see happen to the teacher? Sphokazi: Cries Carol: then we have a negative impact on our society and we see now the consequences of that kind of violence.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): For parents, school is the safest environment for their children, but for some children within the South African school system this comes at a price... the value is the depth of their scars
metadata.Unique Selling Point: For parents, school is the safest possible environment for their children. Some teachers across the country have violated that trust, as the caregiver has become the abuser in some of our schools in South Africa.
metadata.Summary: The Centre for Justice and Crime Prevention’s 2012 School Violence study found that up to 73% of children were still being beaten by their teachers and in 2017, this is still an ongoing crisis in our schools. Recently cellphone footage has surfaced with teachers abusing students in classrooms. For over 20 years corporal punishment has been outlawed as a form of enforcing discipline at schools. But some teachers across South Africa have continued to break the law.
metadata.Further information: Video clips of teachers caning and smacking students in class even going as far as using abusive language to some students have gone viral. In one of the most extreme cases, a video clip shows teachers in the KZN including the school principal sexually assaulting a female student. The department of education has condemned all these acts of violence by the teachers, but is that enough? Tshepiso Monnakgotla mentions that since her child was publicly beaten and humiliated by her school’s food handler, she has had no communication with the department and her child has been suffering ever since with trauma and not being able sleep. Her child needs counseling and the department hasn’t come fourth with any help 3 weeks later. Although a few video clips surfaced, there might be more of these incidents that do not get recorded or reported. But the abuse and videos going viral can cause an even bigger psychological trauma to the children. For many of these children it is trauma that will haunt them for many years to come. How will the department deal with the ongoing issue abuse in schools? Are these acts of violence a product of our state of being as a society and who is accountable when these incidents occur? Carte Blanche investigates Tshepiso Monnakgotla is the mother of a 16-year-old mentally ill girl who was attacked by her school’s food handler in Soweto. Tshepiso says both her and her daughter have been traumatised by the incident to an extent where her daughter doesn’t sleep or eat and she is scared of going back to school. No one can tell her why her daughter was beaten up and the department hasn’t offered her any kind of help with counseling for her daughter. Kristy and Shane Kreusch reported a teacher that has been victimizing and beating up their child to the education department in the Eastern cape but nothing has been done. They even opened a case with the police but they could not be helped. The department told them that the teacher, Ms Hill is a good teacher and perhaps her behavior is linked to her loneliness. The department in the province does however admit to having numerous complains about the teacher but they cannot explain why they haven’t done anything about her. We We speak to the national department of basic education’s spokesperson Mr Elijah Mhlanga who has condemned this acts of abuse on students and says the department will take appropriate actions with these teachers. He speaks of how often such incidents get reported to them and how they normally deal with them. What does this do to the image of the schooling system and most importantly how do they deal with the victims once post the abuse? Carol Bower is an experienced child activist based in Cape Town; she believes condemning these actions is just not enough. More needs to be done to ensure the safety of the children. According to Carol many believe that there is no other way to discipline a child other than a beating and that is not ok. Being hit in childhood has been linked to negative physical, psycho-social, emotional, behavioral and cognitive outcomes. The most disturbing part is this can be linked to the society we live in, with the country having one of the highest levels of violence in the world, it seems our only response to anything we do not like is to lash out. We also speak to parents of a pupil that was beaten up by a teacher and her hand is now permanently damaged. Siphokazi tyalidikazi is currently 15 years of age. When she was 13 her teacher beat her up for not finishing her homework and now her right hand is permanently disabled. She can no longer write with her right hand as a result and had to adjust to write with her left. The teacher that abused her was fined and allowed to nget back to work. She had to change schools because once her parents pressed charges she got victimized at the school by teachers at emfuleni primary school. The parents are now suing the department of education and holding them accountable for the incident. This is currently an ongoing case. Themba Ndlovu of the South African council of educators believes that this is a huge dent to the profession and creates a bad image for profession. The council is responsible for investigations into these incidents and according to Themba they have received 21 complaints of sexual assault from April this up to now, this according to Themba is one too many and needs to stop. The council is engaging with stakeholders and teachers unions to discourage corporal punishment and any kind of abuse, as they believe it will take a collective to eradicate this behavior.
